top_choice_rationale: Optical lattice clocks pair one clear idea, trapping neutral atoms at a magic wavelength so the light shift cancels and many atoms can be interrogated, with the strongest independent confirmation on the table: clocks built separately in several countries agree near 1e-18. The two-name allocation (Katori for the concept and first demonstration, Ye for record accuracy and stability) maps onto what was actually done and the citation can be drawn narrowly around the magic-wavelength lattice, which separates it from the 2005 comb and 2012 ion-control prizes. P001 is a strong, legitimate second choice, with the third seat and twist-angle disorder as my remaining reservations, and I would rather award it than no one.
recusal_note: none apparent from profile; as an atomic physicist at Lund I may be inclined toward lattice clocks, and my WACQT role overlaps institutionally with Chalmers, but I have no tie to Katori, Ye, MacDonald, Bistritzer or Jarillo-Herrero
